“That night the Baron dreamed of many sorrows;
And all his warrior guests, with shapes and shadows
Of witches, demons, and great coffin-worms,
Were long tormented by nightmares.”
Keats

Unhappy is anyone whose childhood memories bring only fear and sadness. Wretched is anyone who looks back on lonely hours in vast, gloomy rooms with brown wall hangings and maddening rows of ancient books; or on fearful vigils in dim groves of grotesque, gigantic trees, tangled with vines, silently waving their twisted branches high overhead. This was the fate the gods gave me—to me, bewildered and disappointed, barren and broken. Yet I am strangely content. I cling desperately to those withered memories whenever my mind threatens, for a moment, to reach beyond them to the other.

I do not know where I was born, except that the castle was endlessly old and endlessly horrible. It was full of dark passages and high ceilings where the eye could find only cobwebs and shadows. The stones of the crumbling corridors always seemed hideously damp. Everywhere there was a cursed smell, like the piled-up corpses of generations of the dead. It was never light, so sometimes I lit candles and stared steadily at them for relief. There was no sunlight outside either, for the terrible trees rose far above the highest tower I could reach. One black tower reached above the trees into the unknown sky beyond, but it was partly ruined. The only way up was an almost impossible climb along the sheer wall, stone by stone.

I must have lived there for years, but I cannot measure the time. Beings must have cared for my needs, yet I cannot remember any person but myself, or anything living except the silent rats, bats and spiders. I think whoever nursed me must have been shockingly old. My first idea of a living person was something mockingly like myself, yet distorted, shrivelled and decaying like the castle. I saw nothing grotesque in the bones and skeletons scattered through some of the stone crypts deep among the foundations. Strangely, I associated them with everyday life. They seemed more natural than the coloured pictures of living beings I found in many of the mouldy books. Those books taught me everything I know. No teacher encouraged or guided me. I cannot remember hearing a human voice in all those years—not even my own. Although I had read about speech, it never occurred to me to try speaking aloud. I gave no more thought to my appearance. There were no mirrors in the castle, and I simply assumed by instinct that I resembled the young figures drawn and painted in the books. I felt young because I remembered so little.

Outside, across the foul moat and under the dark, silent trees, I often lay for hours dreaming of what I had read. Longingly, I pictured myself among cheerful crowds in the sunny world beyond the endless forest. Once I tried to escape from the forest. But the farther I went from the castle, the deeper the shadows grew, and the more the air filled with brooding fear. I ran frantically back, afraid of losing my way in a maze of dark silence.

Through endless twilights I dreamed and waited, although I did not know what I was waiting for. Then, in that shadowy solitude, my longing for light became so desperate that I could no longer rest. I raised my hands in appeal to the one black, ruined tower that reached above the forest into the unknown sky. At last I decided to climb it, even if I fell. It would be better to glimpse the sky and die than to live without ever seeing daylight.

In the damp twilight I climbed the worn, ancient stone stairs until they ended. After that I clung precariously to small footholds leading upwards. That dead cylinder of stone, without stairs, was ghastly and terrible: black, ruined, deserted, and sinister with startled bats whose wings made no sound. But the slowness of my progress was more ghastly and terrible still. However far I climbed, the darkness above me never thinned. A new chill struck me, as though from haunted, age-old mould. I shivered, wondering why I did not reach the light, and would have looked down if I had dared. I imagined that night had suddenly fallen. With one free hand I searched in vain for the recess of a window, hoping to look out and up and judge how high I had climbed.

Then, after what seemed an eternity of fearful, blind crawling up that inward-curving, desperate precipice, my head touched something solid. I knew I must have reached the roof, or at least some kind of floor. In the dark, I raised my free hand and tested the barrier. It was stone and would not move. Then I made a deadly circuit of the tower, clinging to whatever holds the slimy wall offered, until at last my searching hand found a part of the barrier that gave way. I turned upwards again, pushing the slab or door with my head while I used both hands for the fearful climb. No light appeared above. But as my hands reached higher, I knew my climb had ended for the moment. The slab was a trapdoor opening onto a level stone surface broader than the tower below—surely the floor of some lofty, spacious lookout room. I crawled through carefully and tried to keep the heavy slab from falling shut behind me, but failed. As I lay exhausted on the stone floor, I heard the eerie echoes of its fall. I hoped I could force it open again when I needed to.

Believing I was now at an enormous height, far above the forest’s cursed branches, I dragged myself up and felt around for windows. I wanted to see, for the first time, the sky and the moon and stars I had read about. But everywhere I was disappointed. All I found were vast marble shelves holding hateful, oblong boxes of a disturbing size. I thought more and more, wondering what ancient secrets might linger in this high room, cut off for so many ages from the castle below. Then my hands unexpectedly found a doorway, with a stone door roughened by strange carving. I tried it and found it locked. But with a supreme burst of strength I overcame every obstacle and pulled it open towards me. As I did, I felt the purest joy I have ever known. The radiant full moon shone peacefully through an ornate iron grille and down a short stone passage of steps rising from the doorway. I had never seen it before, except in dreams and in vague visions I dared not call memories.

Now imagining that I had reached the very top of the castle, I began to rush up the few steps beyond the door. But a cloud suddenly covered the moon, and I stumbled, then felt my way more slowly through the dark. It was still very dark when I reached the grille. I tested it carefully and found it unlocked, but did not open it, afraid of falling from the astonishing height I had climbed. Then the moon came out.

The most diabolical shock of all is the utterly unexpected and grotesquely unbelievable. Nothing I had suffered before could compare with the terror of what I now saw, or the bizarre wonders that sight implied. The sight itself was as simple as it was staggering. Instead of a dizzying view of treetops from a great height, I saw through the grille solid ground stretching around me at my own level. Marble slabs and columns decorated and varied its surface. An ancient stone church overshadowed it, its ruined spire gleaming ghostlike in the moonlight.

Half conscious, I opened the grille and staggered onto a white gravel path that ran in two directions. Stunned and confused as my mind was, it still held its frantic hunger for light. Not even the fantastic marvel I had encountered could stop me. I neither knew nor cared whether this was madness, a dream or magic. At any cost, I was determined to look upon brightness and joy. I did not know who or what I was, or what my surroundings might be. But as I stumbled on, I became aware of a kind of fearful, buried memory that made my route less than entirely accidental. I passed under an arch, out of that place of slabs and columns, and wandered through open countryside. Sometimes I followed the visible road. At other times I strangely left it to cross meadows where only scattered ruins suggested that a forgotten road had once passed. Once I swam across a swift river, where crumbling, mossy stonework marked a bridge long vanished.

More than two hours must have passed before I reached what seemed to be my destination: an ancient, ivy-covered castle in a densely wooded park. It was maddeningly familiar, yet full of bewildering strangeness. The moat had been filled in, and some towers I knew had been demolished, while new wings confused the eye. But what interested and delighted me most were the open windows, gloriously blazing with light and sending out the sounds of the happiest revelry. I approached one and looked inside. A strangely dressed company was making merry and talking brightly together. I had apparently never heard human speech before and could only vaguely guess what was being said. Some faces held expressions that stirred incredibly distant recollections. Others were utterly unfamiliar.

I stepped through the low window into the brilliantly lit room, passing in that step from my one bright moment of hope into my darkest spasm of despair and understanding. The nightmare came quickly. As I entered, one of the most terrifying scenes I had ever imagined unfolded at once. I had barely crossed the sill when a sudden, unannounced fear of hideous intensity seized the whole company. It twisted every face and drew horrible screams from almost every throat. Everyone fled. In the uproar and panic, several people fainted and were dragged away by their frantically fleeing companions. Many covered their eyes and plunged blindly and clumsily towards escape, knocking over furniture and stumbling against walls before reaching one of the many doors.

The screams were shocking. As I stood alone and bewildered in the brilliant room, listening to their fading echoes, I trembled at the thought of what might be lurking unseen nearby. At first glance the room seemed deserted. But as I moved towards an alcove, I thought I sensed a presence—a hint of movement beyond a golden-arched doorway leading to another, rather similar room. Approaching the arch, I began to make out the presence more clearly. Then, with the first and last sound I ever made—a ghastly howl that revolted me almost as deeply as its foul cause—I saw, in full and dreadful detail, the inconceivable, indescribable, unmentionable monstrosity whose mere appearance had turned a merry company into a herd of frantic fugitives.

I cannot even suggest what it looked like. It combined everything unclean, uncanny, unwelcome, abnormal and hateful. It was the ghoulish shadow of decay, ancient age and desolation; a rotting, dripping phantom of some unwholesome revelation; the terrible exposure of what the merciful earth should always conceal. God knows it was not of this world—or no longer of this world. Yet to my horror, in its eaten-away outline and exposed bones, I saw a leering, repulsive mockery of the human form. Its mouldy, disintegrating clothes had an unspeakable quality that chilled me even more.

I was almost paralysed, but still managed a feeble attempt to escape. I stumbled backwards, unable to break the spell in which the nameless, voiceless monster held me. My eyes, bewitched by the glassy eyes staring loathsomely into them, refused to close. Mercifully, they had blurred, so that after the first shock I saw the terrible thing only indistinctly. I tried to raise a hand to block the sight, but my nerves were so stunned that my arm could not fully obey me. The attempt was enough to upset my balance. I had to stagger forward several steps to keep from falling. As I did, I became suddenly, agonisingly aware of how close the rotting thing was. I half imagined I could hear its hideous, hollow breathing. Nearly mad, I could still throw out a hand to keep back the stinking apparition pressing so near. Then, in one shattering second of cosmic nightmare and hellish accident, my fingers touched the monster’s rotting, outstretched paw beneath the golden arch.

I did not scream. But all the fiendish ghouls that ride the night wind screamed for me, as in that same second a single, fleeting avalanche of soul-destroying memory crashed into my mind. In that second I knew everything that had been. I remembered beyond the dreadful castle and the trees, and recognised the altered building where I now stood. Most terrible of all, I recognised the unholy abomination leering before me as I drew my tainted fingers away from its own.

But the universe holds comfort as well as bitterness, and that comfort is nepenthe, the draught of forgetfulness. In the supreme horror of that second, I forgot what had horrified me. The burst of dark memory vanished in a confusion of echoing images. In a dream, I fled that haunted, cursed building and ran swiftly and silently through the moonlight. When I returned to the marble-filled churchyard and went down the steps, the stone trapdoor would not move. But I was not sorry, for I had hated the ancient castle and the trees. Now I ride the night wind with mocking, friendly ghouls, and by day I play among the catacombs of Nephren-Ka in the sealed, unknown valley of Hadoth beside the Nile. I know that no light is for me except the moon over the rock tombs of Neb, and no joy except the unnamed feasts of Nitokris beneath the Great Pyramid. Yet in my new wildness and freedom, I almost welcome the bitterness of being an outcast.

For although nepenthe has calmed me, I always know that I am an outsider, a stranger in this century and among those who are still human. I have known this ever since I stretched my fingers towards the abomination inside that great gilded frame—stretched out my fingers and touched a cold, unyielding surface of polished glass.
